title: Pakistan's Army Chief Used Iran Energy Deals to Shield Saudi Defense Pact
excerpt: Field Marshal Asim Munir brokered oil and LNG transit agreements with Iran's IRGC through the Strait of Hormuz while simultaneously deploying troops to Saudi Arabia — a dual strategy that raised questions about Pakistan's neutrality as a US-Iran mediator.
body:
• Pakistan struck bilateral energy deals with Iran — including LNG transit through the Strait of Hormuz — while maintaining a mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia that includes troop and fighter jet deployments.
  • Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir personally engaged with Iranian military commanders, including the IRGC, to ensure energy shipments continued and to prevent Iranian retaliation against Pakistan's Saudi alliance.
  • Analysts question Pakistan's neutrality as a US-Iran mediator, noting its simultaneous military commitments to Riyadh and energy negotiations with Tehran.
  • Pakistan is now seeking a $10 billion US exchange stabilization fund, leveraging its diplomatic goodwill from brokering the US-Iran ceasefire earlier this year.

A Balancing Act in the Gulf

Pakistan's Field Marshal Asim Munir has quietly constructed one of the most complex diplomatic positions in the Middle East: defending Saudi Arabia under a mutual defense pact while cutting energy deals with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which controls up to half of Tehran's oil exports and now oversees transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

https://x.com/TheIranWatcher/status/2080435608527257918

The Pakistan-Saudi Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, signed in September 2025, has resulted in the deployment of Pakistani fighter jets to Saudi Arabia and discussions about stationing thousands of troops, air defense systems, and drones in the kingdom, according to Reuters. After Iran-aligned Houthi forces attacked Saudi Arabia in July 2026, nuclear-armed Pakistan declared it would treat attacks on the kingdom as attacks on itself.

Yet even as those forces deployed, Munir was traveling to Tehran. He visited Iran at least twice during the US-Iran war — in April and May 2026 — holding meetings with President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, and the Iranian armed forces' Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters Commander Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian and Pakistani media.

Oil and LNG as Diplomatic Currency

The energy dimension of this balancing act has proved critical. After the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — which normally carries 20% of the world's crude oil and LNG — Iran shifted from blocking the waterway to controlling it, according to the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.

"Iran has shifted from blocking Hormuz to controlling access to it... Hormuz is no longer a neutral transit route, it is a controlled corridor," said Claudio Steuer of the institute.

Pakistan, heavily dependent on Gulf energy imports and facing surging fuel costs, secured a bilateral agreement with Tehran to allow Qatari LNG tankers to pass through the strait. Two tankers loaded with Qatari LNG headed to Pakistan under this arrangement, Reuters reported in May, citing industry sources. Pakistan had been receiving roughly 10 LNG cargoes a month before the war disrupted flows.

The deals were negotiated through IRGC channels, which now collect tolls of up to $2 million per vessel transiting the strait, according to the Wall Street Journal. Iran's military has declared that coordinated control of Hormuz "will generate revenues for the country up to twice the oil income," Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia told state media.

"He has earned a degree of trust."

— Abdul Basit, fellow at the International Centre for Political Violence and Terrorism Research, on Munir's engagement with Iranian and American officials

Mediator or Interested Party?

Munir's dual role has drawn scrutiny from analysts who question whether Pakistan can credibly mediate the US-Iran conflict while maintaining military commitments to both sides' adversaries.

The Cipher Brief, a US-focused intelligence publication, reported that "much of Munir's mediation process remains opaque," noting that "it is unclear who he engages directly on the Iranian side and whether those figures hold real influence." The publication cited regional intermediaries who described Pakistan's role as "extending beyond simply passing messages," suggesting Munir may be "softening positions, adjusting language, or even creating the impression of agreement before it fully exists."

Reports that Pakistan allowed Iranian military aircraft to shelter on its airbases during the conflict further complicated perceptions of Islamabad's neutrality. Pakistan's army has longstanding institutional ties to Iran's military commanders, and Munir "helped manage and reduce tensions through direct engagement with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps," according to the Wall Street Journal.

Economic Dividends and Diaspora Impact

The diplomatic high-wire act has yielded tangible economic benefits. Pakistan is now negotiating defense-for-energy deals with Kuwait and exploring a mutual defense framework with Turkey and Qatar. S&P Global Ratings upgraded Pakistan to 'B' from 'B-' on July 23 — its first credit upgrade in nine years.

Pakistan's Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb pitched Washington a $10 billion exchange stabilization fund during a visit this week, along with a separate trade-finance facility with the US EXIM Bank. Adeel Malik, an Oxford University associate professor, described the proposed facility as "geopolitical rent" earned from Pakistan's mediation role, according to Reuters.

For the Indian diaspora, Pakistan's deepening military entrenchment in the Gulf raises direct questions about regional stability. India depends heavily on Gulf energy supplies and remittances from its large expatriate workforce in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Kuwait. Any escalation that draws Pakistan's military into a Gulf conflict could disrupt energy markets and the economic security of millions of Indian workers in the region.

What Comes Next

The sustainability of Munir's balancing act remains uncertain. Mounting concerns in Islamabad that the Saudi defense pact could draw Pakistan into direct conflict with Iran have intensified after recent Houthi attacks on the kingdom. Pakistan has said it cannot deploy combat troops at this stage, even as Kuwait seeks a similar security arrangement.

Former diplomat Maleeha Lodhi told the Wall Street Journal that Munir is "the man who's the architect of Pakistan's foreign policy" and "probably the only global figure Trump consistently says positive things about." But the question analysts increasingly ask is whether one general can indefinitely serve as Saudi Arabia's defender, Iran's energy partner, and Washington's backchannel to Tehran — without the contradictions catching up.
